title: Anatomy of a Takeover — How a Virus Is Built and Replicates

info.text: How a virus is built — a genome in a protein coat, sometimes wrapped in stolen membrane — and how it takes a cell over: the lytic timetable from docking to bursting, the genome tricks that decide its first move, and the temperate option to hide in the host's DNA until damage brings it out.

clusters.name: Virion architecture
clusters.fact: A virus particle is a genome wearing a coat: protein subunits stack into a shell, the shell hugs the nucleic acid, and some viruses wrap the whole thing in a membrane stolen from their last host cell.

capsid.text: The protein coat that shelters the genome and carries the shapes a micrograph can sort. Built from many copies of one or a few proteins — an economy of design when your genome is tiny.

capsomere.text: The repeating protein subunit a capsid is built from. Identical capsomeres tile into helices or icosahedra — the reason viral coats look so geometric.

envelope.text: A lipid membrane taken from the host — outer membrane, nuclear membrane, or endoplasmic reticulum — as the virus exits. Its proteins are viral; the lipids are borrowed, which is why soap and alcohol dismantle enveloped viruses so well.

nucleocapsid.text: The genome-plus-capsid unit: what an enveloped virus keeps inside its stolen membrane. Measles and influenza carry it as a helical core; herpes as an icosahedral shell.

virion.text: The complete, infectious particle — the thing that travels between hosts. Outside a cell a virion is inert; the takeover program runs only once it is inside.

info.text: Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites: a virion outside a cell does nothing but wait. Everything here is either genome, coat, or wrapper — no metabolism of its own.

clusters.name: Genome sense and shape
clusters.fact: The genome's sense decides how the cell can read it: one kind of RNA is message-ready the instant it arrives, its mirror image must be copied before anything gets made, and some genomes arrive split into separate pieces.

negative-sense.text: A (−)ssRNA genome is the complement of message: nothing can be made until a virus-carried RNA-dependent RNA polymerase copies it. Measles, influenza, rabies, and Ebola all travel this way.

positive-sense.text: A (+)ssRNA genome reads directly as messenger RNA: the host ribosome starts translating the moment it is in the cytoplasm. Poliovirus and coronaviruses travel this way.

segmented genome.text: A genome split into separate pieces, often one gene each. Influenza carries eight segments — and when two strains coinfect one cell, segments shuffle (reassortment), which is how pandemic flu strains are born.

info.text: Viral genomes are DNA or RNA, never both — except when an enzyme shuttles between the two. Sense describes whether RNA reads as message immediately or must be copied first; it is the core of the Baltimore groups.

clusters.name: Coat architectures
clusters.fact: Micrographs sort virus coats into three great shapes: a stacked helix, a geometric shell built from repeated triangles, and custom machinery — a head bolted to a tail — that no simple formula describes.

complex symmetry.text: Neither helix nor shell: poxviruses with their brick-shaped, many-layered body plan, or T4's icosahedral head on a helical tail with baseplate and fibers — custom machinery built for injection.

helical.text: Identical capsomeres stacked in a ribbon around the genome — tobacco mosaic virus's rigid rod, or the flexible coil inside the measles envelope. Simple, and scalable to any genome length.

icosahedral.text: A shell of twenty triangular faces built from 60 or more capsomeres — the most common animal-virus architecture (adenovirus, poliovirus, herpes). The biggest volume for the fewest parts.

info.text: The coat is the only architecture a virus has, and evolution keeps rediscovering two efficient solutions — the helix and the icosahedron — plus custom machinery where infection demands it.

clusters.name: The lytic program
clusters.fact: A virulent phage runs a fixed timetable: dock on the host, inject the genome, redirect the cell's metabolism, mass-produce parts, assemble new particles, and burst the cell open — about two hundred progeny in twenty-five minutes for T4.

attachment.text: First contact: tail fibers or surface proteins dock on a specific host receptor — the lock-picking that decides which cells a virus can even enter.

biosynthesis.text: The hijack: host nucleic acid is degraded, and the cell's ribosomes and enzymes start making phage DNA and proteins on the virus's schedule — early genes redirect, late genes build parts.

lysis.text: The exit: holins punch holes, endolysin chews the cell wall, and osmotic pressure bursts the cell open, releasing the progeny to find new hosts.

maturation.text: Assembly line: heads are filled with genomes, tails bolt on, and a finished virion snaps together — for T4, roughly two hundred per infected cell in about twenty-five minutes.

penetration.text: The genome goes in — injected through a bacterial cell wall, or by membrane fusion or endocytosis in animal cells. For T4 the sheath contracts and DNA is squirted through the tail; the empty capsid stays outside.

info.text: This is the whole program in five steps — the one-step growth curve every virology student learns. Virulent phages can only run it; temperate ones can choose it.

clusters.name: The hidden option
clusters.fact: A temperate phage can skip the timetable: integrate into the host genome and ride silently through generations — the same strategy carries a different name inside animal cells, and DNA damage is the signal that ends the truce.

induction.text: The end of the truce: UV light or DNA-damaging chemicals trip the cell's SOS response, the prophage excises from the chromosome, and the lytic program begins.

lysogen.text: A bacterial cell carrying a prophage. The prophage's repressor protein both keeps the virus quiet and grants superinfection immunity — protection against new infections by related phages.

prophage.text: The integrated phage genome: dormant, replicated passively with its host at every division, mostly silent. It can carry toxin genes that convert harmless bacteria into killers — lysogenic conversion.

provirus.text: The same trick in animal cells: HIV copies its RNA to DNA and inserts a provirus into a chromosome, where it can hide for years — the reason antiretroviral therapy is lifelong.

info.text: Lysogeny is latency with a bacterial address: the phage genome integrates and mostly turns itself off. Lysogenic conversion shows why it matters — diphtheria, cholera, and botulism toxins are all phage genes riding silent.

bridges.fact: For an enveloped virus, exit and dressing are one act: budding through a host membrane releases the particle while wrapping it in its envelope — which is why 'enveloped versus naked' tracks how a virus leaves.

info.text: Enveloped viruses typically exit by budding or exocytosis; naked viruses usually wait for the cell to burst. The route of exit predicts sensitivity to soap and detergent.

bridges.fact: Sense decides the program's first move: a positive-sense RNA genome can be translated the moment penetration ends, but a negative-sense genome must first be copied by a viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase before biosynthesis can start.

info.text: The Baltimore classification is built exactly on this question: how does each genome type get to messenger RNA? Groups IV and V differ only in the answer.

bridges.fact: Complex symmetry is lytic machinery: T4's tail fibers perform attachment and its contractile sheath drives DNA through the cell wall like a molecular syringe — the head-and-tail shape exists to run the program's opening move.

info.text: T4's contractile sheath was one of the first molecular machines imaged in action; its baseplate senses the cell surface and triggers the tail's collapse.

bridges.fact: Induction is the hinge between the two programs: DNA-damaging stress excises the prophage, and the cell that had been riding silent is thrown straight into the lytic timetable.

info.text: Induction matters beyond the lab: stress-woken prophages in gut and soil bacteria can carry toxin genes and spread them to new hosts by transduction.

lenses.prompt: Which single term names the complete, infectious virus particle rather than one of its parts?
lenses.explanation: The virion is the whole infectious unit — genome, coat, and any wrapper. Capsid is the coat alone, nucleocapsid the coat plus genome, capsomere a subunit of the coat, and envelope just the stolen membrane.

reasons.virion: The whole unit that travels between hosts — everything else here is one of its parts.

lenses.prompt: Which terms describe the genome itself rather than the structures wrapped around it?
lenses.explanation: All three describe the genome itself: how its RNA reads, or whether it travels in pieces. Nucleocapsid and capsomere name hardware — structures built around that information.

reasons.negative-sense: A property of the RNA — it must be copied before it reads.
reasons.positive-sense: A property of the RNA — it reads as message directly.
reasons.segmented genome: How the information is packaged: in separate pieces.

lenses.prompt: Which genome can a host ribosome translate immediately on entry, with no copying step first?
lenses.explanation: A positive-sense RNA genome is already messenger RNA: the host ribosome begins translating it on arrival. A negative-sense genome cannot be read at all until a carried polymerase copies it into message first.

reasons.positive-sense: It reads directly as mRNA — message-ready by definition.

lenses.prompt: Which pairing names the phage shape and the takeover step its contractile tail performs?
lenses.explanation: T4 is the head-and-tail complex, and its opening move is penetration: attachment only docks the fibers — the sheath contraction that drives DNA through the wall is the injection step.

reasons.complex symmetry: The head-and-tail architecture no simple formula describes.
reasons.penetration: The injection step — DNA driven through the cell wall.

lenses.prompt: Which two steps bracket the takeover — its first and its last?
lenses.explanation: Attachment opens the program (docking on the receptor) and lysis closes it (bursting the cell). Penetration, biosynthesis, and maturation run between them.

reasons.attachment: First contact with the host receptor — the program's opening move.
reasons.lysis: The burst that releases progeny — the program's final act.

lenses.prompt: Which hidden-option terms name a state rather than an event?
lenses.explanation: Prophage, provirus, and lysogen all name stable states — an integrated genome or the cell carrying it. Induction is the one event: the stress-triggered switch back to lysis.

reasons.lysogen: The cell that carries the prophage — a state, not a switch.
reasons.prophage: The integrated, silent phage genome — a state.
reasons.provirus: The animal-cell equivalent — also a state.

lenses.prompt: Which connection describes what UV damage does to a cell riding silent with a prophage?
lenses.explanation: The lytic-switch bridge is the hinge between the hidden and burst programs: DNA-damaging stress trips the SOS response, the prophage excises, and the cell is thrown into the lytic timetable. Nothing about lysogeny reverses into a prophage — the switch runs one way.

reasons.the lytic switch: Induction: the prophage excises and the lytic timetable begins.

entries.reason: Neighboring boards in the batch: that one teaches the bacterial cell and its three gene-trading routes (transduction is a phage at work); this one teaches the virus doing it — the same takeover from the virus's side of the encounter.

content.text:
Viruses sit at the edge of what we call alive. A virus particle — a virion — is no more than a genome in a protective coat, sometimes wrapped in a membrane stolen from the last cell it infected. It has no metabolism of its own. Everything a virus "does" is really a program its genome runs inside a host cell, using the cell's own machinery.

The coat is surprisingly mathematical. Identical protein subunits, called capsomeres, tile into one of a few efficient shapes: a helical ribbon, a twenty-faced icosahedral shell, or — for some bacterial viruses — custom machinery with a head, a tail, and fibers that grip the host.

The genome varies more than the coat. Viral genomes may be DNA or RNA, and RNA genomes come in two flavors with opposite first moves: a positive-sense genome is messenger RNA already, readable by the host ribosome the moment it arrives; a negative-sense genome is its mirror image and must be copied before anything can be made. Some genomes travel in segments, which lets related viruses swap parts when they share a cell.

Infection follows a timetable. The virus attaches to a specific receptor, penetrates, redirects the cell to synthesize viral parts, assembles new virions, and releases them — often by bursting the cell. That is the lytic program. But bacterial phages have a second option: integrate into the host genome as a prophage and ride silent for generations — the same strategy animal viruses call a provirus. DNA damage ends the truce, inducing the hidden genome back into the lytic program.

That hidden option is one reason viruses keep reshaping life: silent prophages carry toxin genes — those behind diphtheria, cholera, and botulism — and occasionally wake and pass them to new hosts.
